scenes.head: Modelling principles
scenes.sub: A financial model is a machine for answering one question about the future, and someone else has to trust its answers. Learn how to lay out inputs, calculations and outputs, build the timeline, write one formula per row, and follow the conventions that let a lender check your work.

segs.say: Modelling principles. A financial model is a machine for answering one question about the future, and someone else has to trust its answers. Learn how to lay out inputs, calculations and outputs, build the timeline, write one formula per row, and follow the conventions that let a lender check your work.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Explain what a financial model is, and define the decision and the outputs it must serve before building anything.
Design a model with inputs, calculations and outputs kept apart, and each assumption in one labelled cell.
Construct a timeline of actual and forecast periods, and use flags and month counts for events that start part-way through a year.
Write one consistent formula per row that refers to its inputs instead of typing numbers into it.
Apply the conventions of colour, sign and units that let another person read and check a model.

scenes.head: It is February 2028.

segs.say: It is February 2028. Lantern Coffee Co. has two years of accounts behind it, revenue of $577,860 in 2027, and three things starting this spring: a second kitchen on 1 April, the canned Cold Brew, and a new $60,000 term loan from Coastline Bank to pay for the kitchen. Coastline’s credit officer has one more request before the loan is signed. She wants a five-year forecast, 2028 to 2032, showing that Lantern can make the monthly payments and keep its current ratio at 1.2 or more, the condition written into the loan. Ana has a spreadsheet of the 2027 figures and a head full of plans. This course turns them into a model the bank can rely on.

scenes.head: This first lesson is about how a model is built, before any forecasting.

segs.say: This first lesson is about how a model is built, before any forecasting. A model that gives the right answer once but cannot be checked, changed or explained is of little use to Coastline, because the credit officer’s job is to ask “what if?” and see what happens.

scenes.head: A financial model is a set of linked calculations that represents a business’s finances and answers questions about its future.

segs.say: A financial model is a set of linked calculations that represents a business’s finances and answers questions about its future. Its parts are assumptions about the future (how fast sales grow, what things cost, what the loan’s interest rate is), the arithmetic that turns those assumptions into forecast statements, and the results someone will act on. A three-statement model, the kind this course builds, forecasts the income statement, the balance sheet and the cash flow statement together, linked so that a change in one assumption flows through all three.

scenes.head: Every useful model starts from a question, not from a template.

segs.say: Every useful model starts from a question, not from a template. Coastline’s question is narrow: will Lantern have the cash to pay the loan, and will it meet its covenant at every year end? A potential investor would ask what the business is worth. Ana herself wants to know whether she can afford to pay herself more in 2029. The same business can need three different models, or one model with three sets of outputs. Writing the question down first decides which outputs the model must produce, and from those, which calculations and inputs it needs.

scenes.head: Work backwards from the decision

segs.say: Work backwards from the decision. Name the decision, then the outputs that inform it, then the calculations that produce those outputs, then the inputs those calculations need. Build in the opposite order, inputs first, but plan in this one. Anything that serves no output can be left out.

scenes.head: The most important design rule is to keep three kinds of cell apart.

segs.say: The most important design rule is to keep three kinds of cell apart. Inputs are the numbers you type: last year’s accounts, growth rates, prices, the loan’s rate and term. Calculations are formulas that turn inputs into forecasts: revenue, costs, the balance of the loan at each year end. Outputs are the few results someone looks at: the forecast statements, the current ratio each year, the cash at its lowest point. Information flows one way, from inputs through calculations to outputs, and never back.
The three parts of Lantern’s model. Inputs are typed once; calculations refer to them; outputs summarise the calculations for the person deciding.

scenes.head: Keeping them apart has three practical benefits.

segs.say: Keeping them apart has three practical benefits. Each assumption sits in one cell, so changing it once changes it everywhere: when Coastline asks what happens if online sales grow 5% a year instead of 12%, Ana changes one cell, not forty. Inputs can be listed in one place with their sources, so a reader can judge them. And a reader can follow any result back to the inputs that drive it, which is how a model is checked.

scenes.head: A model’s periods run across the columns and its line items down the rows.

segs.say: A model’s periods run across the columns and its line items down the rows. Lantern’s model has one column for each year: 2026 and 2027 are actual results, marked A, and 2028 to 2032 are estimates, marked E. Every column covers the same length of time, here a calendar year ending 31 December, and its heading says which. Periods that are not all the same length (a 10-month first year, say) are a common source of silent errors, because a growth rate applied to a short year understates everything that follows.

scenes.head: Lantern has exactly that problem.

segs.say: Lantern has exactly that problem. Its two cafés opened on 1 March 2027 and traded for ten months, so their 2027 sales of $236,000 are not a year’s sales. Before growing them, the model annualises them: 236,000 × 12 ÷ 10 = 283,200 dollars a year. The opposite problem arises when something starts part-way through a forecast year. The second kitchen opens on 1 April 2028, so it trades for nine months of 2028. A model handles this with a flag, a row that says whether (1 or 0), or for how many months, the kitchen is open in each period, multiplied into every kitchen line. Change the opening date and every kitchen figure moves with it.

scenes.head: In a well-built model every forecast cell in a row holds the same formula, copied across.

segs.say: In a well-built model every forecast cell in a row holds the same formula, copied across. Online revenue for 2028 is last year’s online revenue grown by the 2028 growth rate; online revenue for 2029 is the 2028 figure grown by the 2029 rate; and so on. Written once with the right references and filled to the right, the formula is identical in structure in every column, so checking one cell checks the row.

scenes.head: The opposite is a hard-coded number: a value typed into a cell, or into a formula, where a reference to an input belongs.

segs.say: The opposite is a hard-coded number: a value typed into a cell, or into a formula, where a reference to an input belongs. A forecast that says =C6*1.12 works today, but the 12% is now hidden inside a formula; when the assumption changes, someone has to find every formula that contains it. Worse is a forecast cell that holds a typed number, such as 231,000, with no formula at all. It looks the same as its neighbours until an input changes and it does not.

scenes.head: Filling a formula across a row moves its references.

segs.say: Filling a formula across a row moves its references. A relative reference such as C6 moves with the formula, so in the next column it becomes D6: exactly what “last year’s value” needs. An input that every year shares, such as the cost of goods as a share of sales, must not move, so it is absolute: $B$4. A row of yearly inputs, such as the growth rate for each year, needs the column to move but the row to stay: the mixed reference D$3. Getting these right is what makes one formula per row possible.
Ways to write Lantern’s 2028 online revenue (2027 actual in C6, growth rates for 2028–2032 in D3:H3)

chapters.title: Conventions that let others read the model

scenes.head: Models are read by people who did not build them, so the profession uses shared conventions.

segs.say: Models are read by people who did not build them, so the profession uses shared conventions. The most widespread is colour: blue text for inputs, black for formulas, and green for formulas that pull a value from another sheet or file. A reader can see at a glance what was typed and what was calculated, and a blue number in the middle of a forecast row is an immediate warning. Lantern’s model also shades input cells, so the credit officer knows exactly which cells she may change.

Signs. Decide once whether costs are shown as positive numbers that are subtracted, or as negatives that are added, and keep to it. Lantern’s model shows revenues and costs as positive numbers and subtracts costs, as the income statement does; in the cash flow statement, cash going out is negative.
Units. State the unit in each label or heading (“$”, “cans”, “%”), and do not mix units in one row. If a model is in thousands of dollars, say so at the top of every sheet.
Labels. Every row has a label in the left column that says what it is; inputs say where they came from (“F03 accounts”, “Ana’s estimate”, “Coastline’s term sheet”).
Short formulas. A formula that needs a paragraph to explain should be broken into steps on separate rows. Long nested formulas are where errors hide.

scenes.head: The conventions are summarised in published standards.

segs.say: The conventions are summarised in published standards. The ICAEW Financial Modelling Code, from the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, is a principles-based guide for anyone who builds or uses models. The FAST Standard (its letters stand for Flexible, Appropriate, Structured and Transparent) is more detailed and prescriptive, with rules down to the level of individual formulas. Neither is a law. Large lenders and investors often expect a model to follow one of them, or a house style like it, before they will rely on it.

chapters.title: The layout of a three-statement model

scenes.head: Professional models are usually split into sections, often one per worksheet, in the order the calculations flow.

segs.say: Professional models are usually split into sections, often one per worksheet, in the order the calculations flow. A typical order is shown below. Lantern’s model is small enough for one sheet with these sections stacked down the page, which is how this course builds it. The spreadsheet on this site has no references between sheets, and a single sheet makes the links easier to see.
Cover and contents: what the model is for, who built it, the version and date, and the units.
Inputs: every assumption, with its source. History is input too: the actual accounts are typed in, or linked from the accounting system.
Revenue and cost build-ups: the forecasts of each revenue line and cost, from their drivers (lesson 3).
Schedules: working capital, capital spending and depreciation, and debt (module 2).
The three statements: income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement, built from the lines above.
Outputs: ratios and covenant tests, valuation, scenarios and a one-page summary (module 3).
Checks: the balance sheet balances, cash on the balance sheet equals cash from the cash flow statement, and other tests that should always be zero.

chapters.title: Errors by design, and how to avoid them

scenes.head: Most model errors are not arithmetic mistakes but structural ones: a hard-coded number, a reference that moved when it should not have, a total that…

segs.say: Most model errors are not arithmetic mistakes but structural ones: a hard-coded number, a reference that moved when it should not have, a total that misses a row, a part year treated as a full one. They are prevented more by layout than by care. One input in one place means there is nothing to forget to update. One formula per row means one cell to check per row. A check row that must always be zero, such as total assets minus total liabilities and equity, turns a silent error into a visible one. Module 3 returns to reviewing a model in detail.

scenes.head: One structural trap deserves a warning now.

segs.say: One structural trap deserves a warning now. Interest on a loan depends on the loan’s balance, and if a model also lets the balance depend on interest (by borrowing to pay it, say), the formulas form a loop: a circular reference. Spreadsheets can iterate to a solution, but circular models are fragile and hard to check. Module 2 avoids the loop by charging interest on the balance at the start of each year, a common simplification that this course states wherever it is used.

scenes.head: A model is not a forecast of the truth

segs.say: A model is not a forecast of the truth. Every number in Lantern’s forecast years is a consequence of Ana’s assumptions, not a prediction that will come true. A model’s value is that it makes the assumptions explicit, shows their consequences consistently, and lets anyone change them. Treat its outputs as “what follows if”, and test them with scenario analysis before relying on them.

scenes.head: Growing a line by a rate for each year

segs.say: Growing a line by a rate for each year: Xₜ = Xₜ₋₁ (1 + gₜ).
Xₜ: The line item in year t (online revenue, say) ($).
Xₜ₋₁: The same line in the year before ($).
gₜ: The growth rate assumed for year t, an input.
It assumes this: The years are the same length; the growth rate is for the year being forecast, not the one before.
In a spreadsheet: =C6*(1+D$3), filled right.

scenes.head: Annualising a part year

segs.say: Annualising a part year: Annual amount = Amount for m months × 12/m.
m: The number of months the amount covers (months).
It assumes this: The months that are missing would have looked like the months observed (no strong seasonality).

scenes.head: A part-year amount from a month count

segs.say: A part-year amount from a month count: Amountₜ = Annual amountₜ × (Months openₜ)/12.
Months openₜ: How many months of year t the activity runs (a flag row: 0 to 12) (months).
Annual amountₜ: What the activity would bring in or cost in a full year ($).
It assumes this: The activity runs evenly through the months it is open.
The second kitchen: open 9 months of 2028, 12 of each later year.

chapters.title: Example: Turning a typed forecast into a driven one

scenes.head: Turning a typed forecast into a driven one

segs.say: Ana’s first spreadsheet shows online sales of $187,500 for 2027 and, for 2028 to 2030, three numbers she worked out on a calculator: $210,000, $231,000 and $249,480. Her assumptions were growth of 12%, 10% and 8%. Rebuild the row so that it is driven by the assumptions, with the 2027 actual in C6 and the growth rates in D3:F3.

scenes.head: Turning a typed forecast into a driven one

segs.say: Step 1. Put each assumption in its own input cell: 12% in D3, 10% in E3 and 8% in F3, in blue, labelled “Online sales growth (Ana’s estimate)”.
Step 2. Write one formula for 2028 that grows last year by this year’s rate: =C6*(1+D$3). It gives 187,500 × 1.12 = 210,000.

Step 3. Fill it right to F6. The relative C6 becomes D6 and E6 (last year each time); the mixed D$3 becomes E$3 and F$3 (this year’s rate). 2029: 210,000 × 1.10 = 231,000; 2030: 231,000 × 1.08 = 249,480.
Step 4. Test it: change E3 to 5%. The 2029 and 2030 figures must change and 2028 must not. A typed number would not have moved.

scenes.head: Turning a typed forecast into a driven one

segs.say: The same three figures, $210,000, $231,000 and $249,480, now produced by =C6*(1+D$3) filled across, with the growth rates in their own input cells.
Nothing changed on screen, which is the point: the difference only shows when an assumption changes. Ana can now answer “what if online growth is lower?” by changing one cell.

chapters.title: Example: Three errors in a borrowed model

scenes.head: Three errors in a borrowed model

segs.say: A friend’s template forecast Lantern’s café and online sales. It gave café sales of $245,440 for 2028 and online sales of $210,000, $231,000 and $254,100 for 2028–2030, from the inputs above (café growth 4% in 2028; online growth 12%, 10%, 8%). Ana suspects errors. The formulas are: café 2028 =C5*(1+D$2) with C5 holding 2027’s $236,000; online 2028 =C6*(1+D$3); online 2029 the typed number 231000; online 2030 =E6*(1+E$3). Find each error and its effect.

scenes.head: Three errors in a borrowed model

segs.say: Step 1. Café sales: the formula is fine, but it grows a ten-month figure. 236,000 × 1.04 = 245,440, a year forecast from ten months. Annualise first: 236,000 × 12 ÷ 10 = 283,200, then grow: 283,200 × 1.04 = 294,528. The template understates 2028 café sales by 49,088 dollars, and every later year by more.

Step 2. Online 2029: the typed 231,000 is the right number today, but it is hard-coded. If the 2028 or 2029 growth input changes, 2029 will not move, and neither will anything grown from it. Replace it with =D6*(1+E$3).

Step 3. Online 2030: =E6*(1+E$3) refers to 2029’s growth rate (column E) instead of 2030’s (column F). It gives 231,000 × 1.10 = 254,100 instead of 231,000 × 1.08 = 249,480: 4,620 dollars too high. The formula in 2030 should be =E6*(1+F$3), the same structure as the row’s other cells.

Step 4. Check by structure, not by number: with one formula per row, every forecast cell in the row should look the same when shown as formulas (Show Formulas in Excel). The two online errors are visible at once; the café error needs knowledge of the business.

scenes.head: Three errors in a borrowed model

segs.say: Three errors: a part year grown as if it were a full year (2028 café sales $49,088 too low), a hard-coded 2029 online figure, and a 2030 formula pointing at the wrong year’s growth ($4,620 too high).

Two of the errors are structural and a formula view finds them in seconds; the third is a modelling error that only understanding the history catches. Lesson 2 is about exactly that kind of understanding.

chapters.title: Example: Designing the model Coastline asked for

scenes.head: Designing the model Coastline asked for

segs.say: Coastline wants to know whether Lantern can pay the $60,000 loan and keep its current ratio at 1.2 or more at every year end from 2028 to 2032. Plan the model before building it: the outputs, the calculations they need, the inputs, and the timeline.

scenes.head: Designing the model Coastline asked for

segs.say: Step 1. Outputs, from the question: the loan’s balance and payments each year; cash at each year end; the current ratio at each year end (Coastline tests it every quarter end; an annual model shows the year ends, and module 2 looks at the quarters between); the forecast income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement that produce them; and a check that the balance sheet balances.

Step 2. Calculations, working back: the current ratio needs current assets and current liabilities, so the model needs a working capital schedule and the current portion of each loan; cash needs a cash flow statement; the loan needs a debt schedule; profit needs revenue and cost forecasts; depreciation needs a capital spending schedule.

Step 3. Inputs: the 2026 and 2027 accounts (history); for each revenue line, a driver and a growth or price assumption; cost shares and fixed costs; days of receivables, inventory and payables; capital spending and asset lives; the loan’s amount, rate and term (Coastline’s term sheet); the tax rate; and Ana’s pay and dividend plans.

Step 4. Timeline: seven yearly columns, 2026A and 2027A then 2028E to 2032E, years ending 31 December. A months-open row for the second kitchen holds 9 in 2028 and 12 after, so the kitchen’s first-year revenue is $150,000 × 9 ÷ 12 = $112,500 in 2028.

scenes.head: Designing the model Coastline asked for

segs.say: A one-sheet, three-statement model with an inputs block, revenue and cost build-ups, three schedules, the linked statements, a covenant output row and a check row, over 2026A–2032E.

Planning from the question keeps the model as small as the decision allows. A valuation is not needed for Coastline’s question, but module 3 adds one because Hollis Avery, the investor buying 30% of Lantern, will ask a different question of the same forecast.

scenes.head: Lantern’s model: an extract (figures from the case; growth rates are Ana’s estimates)

segs.say: A small piece of Lantern’s model: the inputs are the shaded cells. Change the online growth rates or the café growth and watch every later year move. Switch on Show formulas to see one formula per row. Then try the error from the challenging example: type 236000 into the café base (B4) and see how far 2028 falls. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Typing numbers into formulas

segs.say: Typing numbers into formulas. A formula such as =C6*1.12 hides an assumption where nobody will find it. Put every assumption in an input cell and refer to it; the only numbers in a formula should be constants that can never change, such as the 12 in “× 12 ÷ 10”.

scenes.head: A different formula in every column

segs.say: A different formula in every column. Patching one year by hand, or writing a slightly different formula in one column, breaks the rule that checking one cell checks the row. If a year genuinely needs different treatment, give it an input (a flag, a month count) and keep the formula the same.

scenes.head: Anchoring the wrong part of a reference

segs.say: Anchoring the wrong part of a reference. Filled right, =C6*(1+$D$3) uses 2028’s rate for every year and =C6*(1+D3) drifts down the page when filled down. Ask of each reference: should it move across, down, both or neither? Yearly inputs in a row need D$3.

scenes.head: Growing a part year as if it were a full year

segs.say: Growing a part year as if it were a full year. A business that opened part-way through the last actual year has a short year in the history. Annualise it (amount × 12 ÷ months) before applying growth, and say so in the label.

scenes.head: Building before knowing the question

segs.say: Building before knowing the question. Starting from a template produces a large model that may still not answer the question asked (Coastline’s covenant, say). Write down the decision and the outputs first; they decide what the model needs.

scenes.head: Mixing units and signs

segs.say: Mixing units and signs. A row with some costs negative and some positive, or one figure in thousands among dollars, adds up wrongly without any error message. State the unit and the sign convention once, at the top, and follow it everywhere.

scenes.head: At a bank like Coastline, the credit officer who receives Lantern’s model does not start with its answers.

segs.say: At a bank like Coastline, the credit officer who receives Lantern’s model does not start with its answers. She starts with its inputs. Are the growth rates plausible against the history? Are the cost shares close to what the accounts show? Is the loan in the model the loan in the term sheet? Then she changes them: online growth halved, the kitchen opening three months late, costs 5% higher. A model built on the principles in this lesson answers each of those questions in seconds and shows the effect on the current ratio. A model with hard-coded numbers gives the same answer whatever she changes, which tells her it cannot be relied on.

scenes.head: The same habits matter inside a business.

segs.say: The same habits matter inside a business. Ana will update the model every quarter with actual results, replacing estimates with facts. If the forecast years are driven by inputs and the history is in its own columns, that is a matter of typing the new actuals in and rolling the timeline forward. If the forecasts were typed in, it is a rebuild.

scenes.head: Professional modellers are judged less on clever formulas than on whether a stranger can audit their work.

segs.say: Professional modellers are judged less on clever formulas than on whether a stranger can audit their work. In large deals, the lender often pays an independent firm to review the borrower’s model before funds are released, and the first things such a review looks for are the ones in this lesson: hard-coded numbers, inconsistent formulas across a row, inputs mixed into calculations, and checks that do not come to zero.

scenes.head: Ana sets up her sheet before forecasting anything: a cover note saying the model is for Coastline’s loan application, in dollars, for calendar years…

segs.say: Ana sets up her sheet before forecasting anything: a cover note saying the model is for Coastline’s loan application, in dollars, for calendar years; an inputs block with each assumption in blue and its source beside it; and seven year columns, 2026A to 2032E. The next lesson fills the history columns from the accounts.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: A financial model answers a question about the future; write the decision and the outputs down before building anything.
Keep inputs, calculations and outputs apart, with every assumption in one labelled input cell and information flowing one way.

Run time across the columns in periods of equal length, marked actual (A) or estimate (E); annualise part years in the history and use month counts or flags for events that start part-way through a forecast year.
Write one formula per row, filled across, with relative references for last year, mixed references for each year’s inputs and absolute references for inputs every year shares.
Never type a number where a reference to an input belongs: hard-coded numbers are the commonest model error and the hardest to see.
Follow shared conventions (blue inputs, black formulas, consistent signs and units, short formulas) so that another person can read and check the model.
Add check rows that must always be zero, and avoid circular references by design.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
